title: YOU CAN LOVE JESUS AND STILL BE RUNNING FROM HIS CHURCH
paragraphs: YOU CAN LOVE JESUS AND STILL BE RUNNING FROM HIS CHURCH

The uncomfortable truth about Christians who refuse church membership, believers wounded by religion, and the difference between following Jesus alone and following Him faithfully. What Hebrews 10:24–25 and Acts 2:42–47 actually reveal may challenge everything you thought you knew about belonging to the Body of Christ.
There is a Christian somewhere reading this who hasn't stepped inside a church building in years.
And before you judge that person, you need to hear what happened.
They used to be the first to arrive.
They volunteered when nobody else wanted to. They gave when their own bills were waiting. They prayed for people who never once asked how they were doing.
They loved Jesus.
They loved His people.
They believed the church was supposed to be the safest place on earth to bring a wounded soul.
Then something happened.
Maybe a pastor betrayed their trust.
Maybe church members spread the very secrets they had shared in confidence.
Maybe they watched leaders preach holiness from the pulpit while practicing something entirely different behind closed doors.
Or maybe nothing dramatic happened at all.
Maybe they simply grew tired of religious routines that seemed to produce more attendance records than transformed lives.
And one Sunday, they stopped going.
At first, they felt guilty.
Then they felt relieved.
Eventually, they began telling themselves something that sounded completely reasonable.
"I still love Jesus. I still read my Bible. I still pray. I don't need to be a member of a church to be a Christian."
And here is where this conversation becomes uncomfortable.
What if part of that statement is absolutely true, but another part is quietly keeping you from something Jesus never intended you to live without?
Because the question is not simply whether someone can be saved without signing a church membership form.
The deeper question is whether a person can faithfully follow a Savior who is building a people while deliberately refusing meaningful fellowship with those people.
Those are not the same question.
And confusing them can leave us defending a position Scripture never actually commands—or rejecting a responsibility Scripture repeatedly emphasizes.
Before we go any further, something needs to be said clearly.
Jesus Christ does not save people through church membership.
He saves sinners through His grace, received by faith.
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." (Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV)
Not through an attendance sheet.
Not through a membership certificate.
Not through a pastor's approval.
Not through an offering envelope.
Not through a religious organization's recognition.
Through Jesus Christ.
The repentant criminal hanging beside Jesus had no opportunity to attend a membership class, participate in a church meeting, or establish a record of service.
Yet Jesus told him:
"Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." (Luke 23:43, KJV)
His hope rested in Christ, not in a religious institution.
That matters.
Especially to someone who has been made to feel that leaving a particular congregation means leaving God Himself.
It does not.
A church can remove your name from its membership records.
It cannot erase the saving work of Jesus Christ.
But there is another truth we cannot ignore.
The same Jesus who saves us individually calls us into a community where we learn to love, serve, forgive, and grow together.
And that is where Hebrews 10 becomes impossible to dismiss.
The writer of Hebrews says:
Notice what the passage actually says.
It does not say, "Make sure your name appears on an official membership roster."
It does not prescribe a particular denominational structure, membership application, or modern administrative system.
But neither does it say, "As long as you believe privately, gathering with other believers is optional."
The original Greek brings the command into sharper focus.
The word translated "assembling" is ἐπισυναγωγή (episynagōgē), referring to a gathering or assembling together.
The expression translated "not forsaking" includes μὴ ἐγκαταλείποντες (mē enkataleipontes), conveying the idea of not abandoning or neglecting the gathering.
And the word translated "exhorting" is παρακαλοῦντες (parakalountes), which can carry the sense of encouraging, urging, or comforting.
These words matter because the writer's concern is not merely whether Christians occupy the same room.
His concern is whether believers are actively helping one another persevere in faith.
The passage begins with a remarkable command.
"Let us consider one another."
In Greek, the expression includes κατανοῶμεν ἀλλήλους (katanoōmen allēlous).
It calls believers to pay thoughtful attention to one another.
Think about that.
Not simply noticing who attended.
Not checking who contributed financially.
Not counting how many people showed up for the Sunday photograph.
Actually considering one another.
Recognizing when someone is struggling.
Encouraging someone whose faith is weakening.
Helping someone resist temptation.
Stirring one another toward love and good works.
That is a far more demanding picture of church life than merely occupying a chair every Sunday.
And it raises a question many of us would rather avoid.
If nobody in your Christian life knows when you are spiritually falling apart, who is helping you carry the burden?
You can listen to excellent sermons online.
You can follow gifted Bible teachers.
You can read Scripture every morning.
You can pray in your bedroom with genuine tears.
Those practices can be deeply valuable.
But a sermon cannot personally notice when you have begun withdrawing from everyone.
A prerecorded message cannot sit beside you at the hospital.
A devotional cannot independently recognize that your marriage is collapsing.
An online audience cannot automatically provide the mutual responsibility and personal care that Scripture describes.
Digital fellowship can be a real blessing, especially for the isolated, disabled, homebound, persecuted, or geographically distant believer.
But consuming Christian content is not automatically the same as belonging to a Christian community.
And following a preacher is not the same as being known by fellow believers.
There is a difference between receiving spiritual information and participating in spiritual family.
Perhaps this is why Acts 2 gives us such a compelling picture of the earliest Christian community.
After Peter preached Christ crucified and risen, thousands received the message and were baptized.
Then Luke describes what followed.
"And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers." (Acts 2:42, KJV)
The Greek expression ἦσαν δὲ προσκαρτεροῦντες (ēsan de proskarterountes) emphasizes their continuing devotion or perseverance.
Their commitment was not a passing emotional response.
They continued.
In the apostles' teaching.
In fellowship.
In breaking bread.
In prayers.
The word for fellowship is κοινωνία (koinōnia).
It speaks of sharing, participation, and communion.
Not merely knowing that other Christians exist.
Not merely enjoying religious company when convenient.
But participating in a shared life centered on Jesus Christ.
And the account becomes even more striking.
"And all that believed were together, and had all things common; And sold their possessions and goods, and parted them to all men, as every man had need." (Acts 2:44–45, KJV)
They were not simply collecting names.
They were sharing burdens.
Their fellowship affected how they treated the hungry, the needy, and the vulnerable.
And Acts 2:46 tells us that they continued together in the temple and broke bread from house to house.
Their spiritual life was not confined to one building.
It extended into their homes.
Their tables.
Their daily relationships.
Their practical responsibilities.
The early church was not defined by a modern membership card.
But it was unmistakably a recognizable, committed community of believers.
That distinction is essential.
Acts 2 describes devoted belonging, even though it does not prescribe every administrative detail of modern formal membership.
And the New Testament gives us more evidence that Christians were expected to belong to identifiable communities.
Paul addressed letters to actual congregations.
Believers were instructed to care for one another.
Church leaders were given responsibility to shepherd God's people.
Hebrews 13:17 speaks about spiritual leaders who watch over souls and must give an account.
First Peter 5:2–3 commands elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, without greed or domination.
First Corinthians 5 describes a congregation exercising discipline within its community.
These instructions assume that believers and leaders can recognize meaningful relationships of responsibility and care.
A shepherd cannot responsibly care for a flock he does not know.
And a Christian cannot fully practice every "one another" command while permanently refusing all meaningful relationships with other Christians.
Yet none of this proves that every believer must participate in one particular modern membership procedure.
Formal membership can be a wise and biblical way for a congregation to clarify commitment, pastoral care, accountability, and responsibility.
But the exact paperwork and administrative process are not directly commanded in Hebrews 10 or Acts 2.
We must not turn a helpful church practice into a condition of salvation.
And we must not use the absence of a membership form in the first century as an excuse to reject the genuine commitments those believers practiced.
There is a difference between lacking a membership certificate and refusing to belong.
A Christian may be faithfully committed to a local congregation without having completed a formal membership process, depending on that church's structure.
A Christian may also be unable to participate regularly because of illness, disability, caregiving responsibilities, persecution, or circumstances beyond their control.
That is not the same as casually abandoning fellowship.
And someone who has escaped spiritual abuse may need time, wise counsel, and a safe environment before becoming deeply involved in another congregation.
God's call to fellowship should never become a weapon used to force wounded people back into harmful situations.
Jesus does not command His sheep to remain under wolves.
He is the Good Shepherd.
He laid down His life for the sheep (John 10:11).
And any church leader who uses biblical authority to manipulate, exploit, threaten, or silence people is acting contrary to the example of Christ.
Spiritual leadership is not ownership.
Accountability is not coercion.
Submission to biblical teaching is not surrendering your conscience to a human being.
A pastor is not your savior.
A denomination is not your redeemer.
And a church institution does not possess the authority to replace the Word of God.
But here is where the conversation becomes personal.
What happens when someone is no longer avoiding a harmful congregation, but avoiding Christian community altogether?
What happens when an understandable wound gradually becomes a permanent wall?
What happens when "I don't trust that church anymore" slowly becomes "I don't need any church at all"?
Pain can explain why we withdraw.
But pain does not always tell us where healing will be found.
And sometimes the walls we build to keep disappointment out also keep genuine love from reaching us.
Perhaps you were hurt by someone who claimed to represent Jesus.
Perhaps you watched religious people act nothing like Him.
Perhaps you prayed for justice and watched the people responsible carry on as though nothing had happened.
You do not need to pretend that it was acceptable.
You do not need to call abuse a misunderstanding.
You do not need to reconcile with an unrepentant abuser or place yourself back under unsafe leadership.
But please do not confuse the failures of people who carry Christ's name with the character of Christ Himself.
Jesus is not guilty of every sin committed by someone who claims to speak for Him.
And His church, though imperfect and often in need of repentance and reform, remains precious to Him.
Paul writes:
That sentence should stop us.
Jesus knew exactly how flawed His people would be.
He knew there would be hypocrisy.
He knew there would be betrayal.
He knew some would seek power instead of service.
He knew congregations would struggle with division, pride, and spiritual immaturity.
The New Testament itself records these failures.
Yet Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
Not because His people were already perfect.
But because He is gracious.
He does not excuse their sins.
He calls them to repentance.
He does not abandon His work of sanctification.
He continues cleansing and transforming His people through His truth.
And perhaps this is where some of us need to examine our own hearts.
Not everyone who stays away from church is rebellious.
But not everyone who stays away is simply wounded, either.
Sometimes the reason is pride.
Sometimes it is an unwillingness to be corrected.
Sometimes we prefer a faith where nobody knows enough about our lives to challenge us.
We want encouragement without accountability.
Teaching without relationships.
Blessing without responsibility.
A Savior who comforts us, but no fellow believers who can confront us when we are drifting.
We want the benefits of belonging to Christ without the inconvenience of loving difficult people.
And if we are truthful, there are moments when other Christians are difficult to love.
They misunderstand us.
They disappoint us.
They disagree with us.
They expose our impatience.
They require forgiveness.
They need mercy when we would rather walk away.
But what if that is part of the reason God calls us into fellowship?
Because patience cannot mature where nobody tests it.
Forgiveness remains theoretical until someone actually wrongs us.
Humility is easy to admire until we are asked to practice it.
And love becomes far more than a beautiful word when we must demonstrate it toward someone who cannot repay us.
Jesus said:
"By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." (John 13:35, KJV)
He did not say the world would recognize His disciples primarily by their membership documents.
But He also did not describe a discipleship that had no practical relationships in which love could be seen.
Love requires people.
Real people.
Not imaginary Christians who always agree with us.
Not flawless believers who never disappoint us.
Actual brothers and sisters in Christ.
And here is a truth that should humble every congregation reading this.
If the church is going to call wounded Christians back into fellowship, it must be willing to become the kind of community that takes their wounds seriously.
Church leaders cannot demand trust while refusing transparency.
Congregations cannot preach forgiveness as an excuse to avoid accountability.
Believers cannot quote Hebrews 10:25 at someone who has been mistreated while ignoring the surrounding command to stir one another toward love and good works.
The call to gather is not permission to control.
It is a call to mutual care.
A healthy church should not merely ask, "Why haven't you been attending?"
It should also be willing to ask, "Have we failed to love you well?"
And when the answer is yes, humility should follow.
Not defensiveness.
Not threats.
Not religious intimidation.
Repentance.
Because the church does not belong to its pastor, its board, its donors, or its most influential families.
It belongs to Jesus Christ.
In Matthew 16:18, Jesus declares:
"I will build my church."
The Greek word translated "church" is ἐκκλησία (ekklēsia), commonly referring to an assembly or congregation.
In the New Testament, the word can refer to particular local congregations or to Christ's people more broadly.
The word itself does not establish a modern membership application process.
But it reminds us that Christ is building a people, not merely collecting isolated admirers.
He is the builder.
He is the head.
He is the foundation of our hope.
And we must be careful not to replace His authority with human traditions.
So can a Christian faithfully follow Jesus without being a formal member of a local church?

Yes, formal membership itself is not an explicit universal requirement for salvation or faithful discipleship. But deliberately rejecting meaningful Christian fellowship, mutual care, and appropriate spiritual accountability is difficult to reconcile with the pattern and commands of the New Testament.
That is the distinction we must preserve.
Not every faithful Christian has a membership card.
But faithful Christianity is not intended to be a permanent life of self-sufficient isolation.
A believer who is seeking a sound congregation is not necessarily forsaking the assembly.
A homebound Christian receiving pastoral care and participating in fellowship as circumstances allow is not necessarily neglecting Christ's people.
A believer who has left an abusive church and is carefully rebuilding trust is not automatically disobedient.
And a congregation meeting in a home is not less biblical simply because it does not own a building.
The New Testament does not make a particular architectural design or administrative system the measure of authentic Christian fellowship.
What matters is whether believers are genuinely living under Christ's Word, growing in love, participating in the life of His people, and practicing the responsibilities Scripture gives them.
For many Christians, formal membership in a biblically faithful local congregation will be a wise and valuable expression of that commitment.
For others, meaningful belonging may exist without that exact administrative form.
But the heart of the matter remains the same.
Are you known?
Are you growing?
Are you learning to serve?
Are you receiving correction when needed?
Are you encouraging others?
Are you participating in the shared life of Christ's people rather than merely observing Christianity from a distance?
And perhaps most importantly:
Are you willing to love the people Jesus loves?
Because it is possible to attend church every week and remain spiritually disconnected.
It is possible to hold an official membership certificate and refuse every meaningful responsibility of Christian fellowship.
It is possible to sit in the same pew for twenty years while never truly bearing another believer's burden.
A signature on a form cannot manufacture genuine discipleship.
And attendance alone cannot prove spiritual maturity.
But neither can private devotion replace every responsibility we have toward one another.
We need both personal communion with God and meaningful fellowship with His people.
We need the secret place of prayer.
And we need brothers and sisters who will pray beside us.
We need Scripture opened in solitude.
And we need Scripture taught, discussed, and lived out in community.
We need moments alone with Jesus.
And we need people who will remind us of His promises when our own strength is failing.
The Christian life is deeply personal.
But it was never designed to be entirely private.
Think about Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
He knew what it meant to fail publicly.
He knew the shame of discovering that his courage was not as strong as he imagined.
But the risen Christ did not leave Peter in the ruins of his failure.
In John 21, Jesus restored him and called him to care for His sheep.
"Feed my sheep." (John 21:17, KJV)
Notice the direction of Peter's restoration.
Jesus did not merely restore Peter to private peace.
He entrusted him with responsibility toward others.
Grace restored a broken disciple and sent him back into a life of service.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Jesus does not save us because we have successfully loved everyone.
He saves us by grace.
Then He teaches us how to love.
He does not forgive us because we have never disappointed His people.
He forgives sinners who come to Him in repentance and faith.
Then He begins transforming how we treat His people.
And this is where our Gospel Warrior message becomes more than a slogan.
The scandal may be what happened inside a church that should have protected you.
The scandal may be the hypocrisy that shattered your trust.
Or perhaps the scandal is something you have been hiding.
Your bitterness.
Your pride.
Your refusal to forgive.
Your habit of using someone else's failure as permission to stop obeying what Christ has clearly taught.
But grace does not merely expose what is broken.
Grace invites us to bring it to Jesus.
Not to excuse sin.
Not to erase consequences.
Not to pretend that repentance is unnecessary.
But to receive the forgiveness and transformation that only Christ can give.
Maybe your next faithful step is not immediately signing a membership form.
Maybe it is finding one mature, trustworthy Christian with whom you can pray.
Maybe it is visiting a biblically sound congregation where leaders demonstrate humility, accountability, and genuine care.
Maybe it is speaking honestly about the church experience that wounded you.
Maybe it is asking God to show you whether your isolation is a necessary season of healing or a wall you have become afraid to leave.
And perhaps, if you are already part of a church, your next step is to notice the person who has quietly disappeared.
Not to shame them.
Not to interrogate them.
Not to send them a verse as though their pain can be solved with one sentence.
But to love them.
To listen.
To ask whether they are safe.
To offer practical help.
To remind them that they matter beyond their attendance and financial contributions.
Because Hebrews 10:24–25 is not simply a command to show up.
It is a call to help one another keep going.
And somebody reading this is barely holding on.
They have not stopped believing in Jesus.
They have simply become exhausted by people who claim to follow Him.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
You are not required to return to a congregation that harmed you.
You are not required to trust a leader who has abused that trust.
You are not required to pretend your wounds have healed when they have not.
But you are invited to keep following Jesus.
And as He leads you forward, do not assume that every Christian community will repeat the failures of the one that hurt you.
There are believers who will pray without gossiping.
There are leaders who will serve without manipulating.
There are congregations that take Scripture seriously and practice accountability.
There are brothers and sisters who understand that love sometimes looks like sitting quietly beside someone who has no strength left to explain their pain.
No congregation will be perfect.
But a healthy church should be marked by a sincere commitment to biblical truth, repentance, humility, safeguarding the vulnerable, and love.
You do not need a perfect church.
You need a community sincerely seeking to follow a perfect Savior.
And if you are reading this while confidently declaring, "I don't need other Christians," consider Paul's words:
"And the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee." (1 Corinthians 12:21, KJV)
Paul was describing the body of Christ.
Different members.
Different gifts.
Different responsibilities.
Yet belonging to one another.
No single member possesses everything the body needs.
And no member should be treated as though they have nothing to contribute.
Perhaps you have been telling yourself that you do not need the church.
But what if someone in the church needs the encouragement God has equipped you to give?
What if your testimony could strengthen a struggling believer?
What if your presence could comfort someone who has been praying not to face another Sunday alone?
What if the spiritual gifts God has given you were never intended to remain permanently hidden?
Christian fellowship is not merely about what we receive.
It is also about what we give.
Not to earn God's acceptance.
But because we have already received His grace.
And if this article has exposed something in your heart, do not rush past it.
Maybe you need to repent of pride.
Maybe you need to grieve a betrayal you have never fully processed.
Maybe you need to stop excusing a harmful religious system.
Maybe you need to stop using the failures of that system to justify abandoning every Christian relationship.
Maybe you need courage to try again.
Or perhaps you are a church leader who needs to ask whether the people under your care are truly being shepherded—or merely counted.
Whatever your situation, bring it into the light of Christ.
He is not threatened by your questions.
He is not confused by your pain.
And He is not asking you to manufacture trust in people who have not demonstrated trustworthiness.
He calls you to trust Him.
To follow His Word.
To walk in repentance.
To receive His grace.
And to learn, in wisdom and love, how to live as part of His people.
If you have never truly surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, church membership cannot save you.
But Jesus can.
His death and resurrection are the foundation of our hope.
He bore our sins, rose from the dead, and calls us to repentance and faith.
The door of grace is not opened by a pastor's signature.
It is opened through the saving work of Christ.
And if you already belong to Him, remember this:
Your salvation is not maintained by a membership certificate.
But your discipleship should increasingly reflect the love, truth, humility, and fellowship He commands.
That is not legalism.
That is learning to follow the One who loved us first.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not a question designed to win an argument.
A question that may help another wounded believer feel less alone.
Have you ever walked away from a church because you were hurt, or have you struggled to find a Christian community where you genuinely belong?
If you feel comfortable, tell us what you learned.
You do not need to disclose private details or identify anyone who harmed you.
Your honest words may remind another person that they are not the only one carrying this struggle.
And if this message brought someone to mind, consider tagging them with kindness. Not to accuse them of abandoning church, but to open a thoughtful conversation.
Not because every reader will agree.
Not because arguments create spiritual growth.
But because somewhere in your circle is a person who has quietly concluded that following Jesus means they must choose between enduring spiritual harm and living completely alone.
They deserve to hear that Scripture offers a more faithful, compassionate, and Christ-centered way forward.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who no longer consider themselves Christians to follow along.
We want people to encounter Jesus Christ—not merely another religious argument.
These resources are intended to encourage Bible study, prayer, repentance, spiritual growth, and a deeper understanding of the Gospel.
They are not a substitute for belonging to a faithful Christian community.
They are tools to help you grow as you follow Jesus.
There is also a practical way to help this ministry continue.
But we want to be biblically clear.
Scripture teaches:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
You do not need to purchase access to God's favor.
You cannot buy spiritual maturity.
But if you believe in the mission and want to help it reach more people, your voluntary support can make a meaningful difference.
It is a practical expression of appreciation for those who choose to stand alongside this work.
Send it to someone who has been struggling with church hurt.
Invite someone to explore the free resources.
Pray that the Gospel will reach people who have stopped believing they can ever belong again.
Financial support is one way to participate.
Prayer, encouragement, sharing, and faithful service are meaningful ways to support Gospel ministry too.
Because the purpose of Gospel Warrior is not to build loyalty to a personality.
It is to point people to Jesus Christ.
The One who forgives sinners.
The One who confronts hypocrisy.
The One who restores the repentant.
The One who cares for wounded sheep.
The One who calls isolated believers toward love without excusing those who have harmed them.
The One who builds His church.
So perhaps the question you should carry away from this article is no longer simply, "Do I have to become a formal church member?"
Perhaps the deeper question is this:
"Lord Jesus, am I allowing You to teach me how to belong to Your people in truth, love, wisdom, and faithfulness?"
That is a prayer worth bringing before Him.
Because one day, the arguments about membership forms and religious labels will fade.
But the love we practiced, the truth we obeyed, the people we served, and the grace we received through Christ will have mattered.
And perhaps the person who once walked away from church in tears will one day find themselves sitting beside another wounded believer, whispering the words they once desperately needed to hear.
"You're welcome here. You can take your time. Let's keep looking to Jesus together."
Not because every wound has disappeared.
Not because every Christian has suddenly become trustworthy.
But because Christ is still at work.
Still redeeming.
Still sanctifying.
Still calling His people to love one another.
And still proving that the failures of human beings do not have the final word over the lives surrendered to Him.
The hands that were wounded by nails are still able to lead wounded people toward grace—and no betrayal committed in His name can erase the love of the Savior who died for them.
